Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: After two years of fighting, what is Ukraine's ability in making its own weapons and ammunition?
Answer: Ukraine’s weapons production ability is close to zero. Not quite zero, but it is essentially working through artisans. What does this mean? It means that the production is being carried out manually and mostly in smaller machine shops. Big factories obviously do not survive long in Ukraine right now, and this severely limits the scale of any production. There are those who would post a picture of a couple of guys in a basement making mortar shells saying this is a booming production. But this is an outright lie and fantasy. This is what a booming production looks like: RDM Danel factory SA Not a couple of people using manual tools in a basement. I don’t know how that isn’t obvious, but apparently it is not. Ukraine is doing pretty well with what they have, but if they were actually booming in military production, they wouldn’t be completely reliant on foreign deliveries now would they. And they are. The reason why Zelensky has been pointing out that without western shells Ukrainian artillery is silent, is because Ukraine is incapable of any relevant production of shells above mortar caliber. Hiding this fact doesn’t help Ukraine, it’s just silly.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Were there any American tanks used in the Battle of Kursk?
Answer: Indeed there was. The battle of Kursk saw vast amounts of Soviet tank reserves being used, which included all kinds of tanks in irregular formations. This included foreign tanks such as the M3 Lee tanks seen above, which was used by some units in the 6th Guards Army. Some M3 Stuart light tanks might also have participated in Kursk. The Soviets were not particularly happy with either of these tanks, the M3 Stuart used high octane aviation fuel, which meant they required a separate fuel supply from all other tanks, additionally it was very poorly armored and armed even compared to the worst Soviet tanks like the T-26. The M3 Lee was better received but the design was very bad as well, with the main gun being fixed in the hull. The M4 Sherman which the Soviets loved had not be delivered yet. It should be noted that British Churchill tanks also participated in Kursk as part of the 5th Guards Tank Army, where they fought against the elite SS Panzer corps. Due to mobility issues the Soviets were not entirely happy with the Churchill, however, the defensive aspects of the tank cannot be denied, and the Churchills were put where the fighting was toughest, and many of them survived the battle. Valentines and Matilda tanks also equipped some units of the Red Army, The Valentine Mk II with it’s 57mm gun, was very well equipped for anti tank fighting for a light tank. The Soviets compared the Valentines to M3 Stuats and T-60/T-70 Soviet light tanks, and fought that the Valentine was pretty well armored, and very well armed, as well has having pretty good off road mobility despite narrow tracks. It was therefore appreciated and used by many Soviet units even quite late in the war, as replacement for other light tanks, including at Kursk.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Are 105mm howitzers used in Ukraine? Do they face the same shortages as 155mm artillery shells? Doesn't NATO have several different 105mm self-propelled guns in storage that could be used in the Ukraine?
Answer: 105mm Howitzers are indeed used in Ukraine, including the M101 seen above. A World War 2 howitzer that the Lithuania graciously donated to Ukraine, though I personally find that rather insulting. Britain supplied the much more modern L118 and eventually the US also gave some L119 which are 105mm howitzers from the 1970s. We do not have a large amount of 105mm SP artillery, very few SP artillery platforms were made during the cold war in NATO, and those which are made now are all exclusively using 155mm ammunition. The reason we gave Ukraine 105mm artillery at all, was because we couldn’t deliver what we promised Ukraine in 155mm. There is also a shortage of the 105mm rounds, because as far as I am aware, they are not produced anymore in the west. We have asked South Korea to give up their ancient reserve arsenal of 3 million 105mm shells for Ukraine, but this stockpile will not be refilled. 105mm shells are not so easy to come by, I suspect we gave them what we had as a stop gap, but for example the EU/Czech initiative to get shells for Ukraine were exclusively 155mm NATO rounds and 122mm Russian rounds. Last I heard the Czech back tracked on this and lowered their promise from 800,000 to 300,000 rounds and no mention of 105mm. The fact that not even the US has anymore stockpiles to send Ukraine of this round and has to ask South Korea, probably means it’s pretty much dry. [Edit] As Austin pointed out, the M119 105mm howitzer is still in service, so we probably do have a production of my 105mm shells, though it appears not to be as big as the 155mm. I apologize for that error.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: I have read in a blog that Russian armoured corps these days love T80 tanks with GT engines and Russia is planning to restart T80 tank production with GTE. Is it true?
Answer: Russian armored troops likely do not hop between tank types, it is better to retain educated crews in the tank they are most familiar with, so most Russian armored troops will not have an educated opinion on the superiority of the T-80 over other Russian tanks. That being said the T-80BVM model appears to be well liked and for good reason. The T-80BVM Obr. 2023 features additional protection, and probably some modifications to make it easier for UVZ to produce. According to Forbes, Alexander Potapov the CEO of the Russian tank factory UVZ, said that they will start building T-80BVM from scratch. It is hard to say if the newest arrivals of T-80BVM Obr. 2023, are scratch build, or upgraded T-80BV, I would assume the latter is still more prominent. But it does seem like the speed of the T-80BVM is desirable so it might indeed already be in production or scheduled for it.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Did Ukraine underestimate Russia’s capabilities or is it the failure of Nato intelligence? What could explain the failure of the Ukrainian counter offensive?
Answer: The offensive was launched in a rushed manner and with a divorce from reality of warfare. Many people in the west and apparently also in Ukraine patted themselves on the back following the successful Ukrainian defensive in the spring of 2022, and the successful Ukrainian offensive in the from September to November in the same year, and many people were talking about various equipment doing wonders to the Russians, but what I really remember from this time was not wonder weapons, it was trucks and trucks and trucks of these bad boys: Mines. Apart from Ukraine using basically the entire arsenal of Soviet TM-62 anti tank mines they had, they were also supplied with mines from Estonia, Germany, France, Sweden, UK and the USA. Furthermore Ukraine heavily used anti-personnel mines, again many left overs from the Soviet Union, probably expending the entire arsenal of PFM-1 mines delivered by BM-27, which was a serious problem for the Russian forces. Additionally, if we remember the initial Russian invasion force was a little over 200,000 strong, the Ukrainian military was mobilized to a strength of nearly 600,000 within a few months, and according to Ukrainian authorities reached about 1 million in total strength by October, including many in the interior of course, not all on the front line. For most of the war, Ukraine has been fighting with a numerical superiority in the area of operation. The entire Russian armed forces in 2022 was 900,000 troops, of which 280,000 were the army, 31,000 in the marine infantry, and 45,000 in the VDV. Which means Russia committed about 55% of their combat troops to the invasion initially. However, by January 2023 the Russian army had increased to 550,000 troops, VDV increased to 50,000 troops, while the marine infantry decreased slightly to 30,000. Either way, the amount of combat troops in the Russian army increased from 356,000 to 630,000. By the summer offensive it is estimated that this number was approaching 1 million. Additionally DPR & LPR and Wagner troops also supported this. In 2022 Ukraine had a reserve of a little under 500,000, while Russia had a reserve of 2 million. By 2023, the Ukrainian manpower reserve was done completely. While the Russians had used only 25% of their reserve, which mainly went into expanding the army. What does all this mean? Because of these 4 reasons, the Ukrainian offensive was doomed from the beginning. We didn’t know just how bad it was until recently, but the failure to break through the minefields in June and July were a bad omen, and after 5 months of continuous assaults Ukraine has lost many of it’s veterans and best trained soldiers. We know that the Ukrainian offensive in the south is ultimately over, because the Ukrainian western trained elite brigades have been moved from offensive actions near Robotino, to defensive actions against Russian attacks in Kupiansk and Avdiivka. The fate of Ukrainian offensive capability relies not only on western arms deliveries, which are severely lacking recently, but also on the ability of Ukraine to recall many of its young people who fled Ukraine as refugees, into coming back to fight. Otherwise Ukraine will eventually face a critical manpower shortage, unless they can win a decisive battle soon, which seems exceedingly unlikely under the current conditions.
